intro: A B♭ bell sounds throughout Le Gibet, Ravel’s setting of Aloysius Bertrand’s gallows at sunset. Chords gather around it and fall away; the bell keeps its dreadful appointment.

sections.label: A · The B♭ bell
sections.mNote: A repeated octave sounds above slow chords

sections.label: B · Chords above and below the bell
sections.mNote: The hands pass the B♭ between them

sections.label: C · A bare melody, without expression
sections.mNote: The bell moves below the exposed upper line

sections.label: Dev · The chords gather again
sections.mNote: Fuller chords return around the unchanged B♭

sections.label: Coda · The bell outlasts the melody
sections.mNote: Low held notes and B♭ remain at the close

cues.title: One note tolls
cues.text: B♭, in octaves, keeps sounding while slow chords move beneath it. Ravel marks the piano Très lent and asks for the soft pedal throughout. The bell has its own rhythm; the other notes lean across it.
cues.evidence: Durand score (1909), plate D. & F. 7207, p. 17: Très lent, Sourdine durant toute la pièce, repeated B♭ octaves. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/6a/IMSLP246875-PMLP02576-Ravel,_Maurice-Gaspard_de_la_nuit_Durand_7207_scan.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A bell beyond the horizon
cues.text: Bertrand’s poem searches among small, horrible sounds: a fly at the dead man’s ear, a spider making his necktie. Then comes the answer: “C’est la cloche qui tinte” — “It is the bell that tolls.” Beyond the town walls, the setting sun reddens the hanging body.
cues.evidence: Aloysius Bertrand, Le Gibet, Gaspard de la nuit, Mercure de France edition (1895), pp. 245–246; our translation. https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Gaspard_de_la_nuit_(%C3%A9d._1895)/Le_Gibet

cues.title: Bertrand, read again
cues.text: Ravel and Ricardo Viñes read Aloysius Bertrand as students, among the Baudelaire, Poe and Mallarmé they devour. A new edition of 1908 sends Ravel back to him. From May to 5 September he writes Gaspard, “three romantic poems of transcendental virtuosity”; Viñes plays it on 9 January 1909.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner’s programme note (https://geraldlarner.com/work/ravel-gaspard-de-la-nuit-1908) gives the student reading with Viñes, the 1908 Mercure de France edition (which he says “must have” revived Ravel’s interest), the composition between May and September 1908 and Ravel’s own phrase. Manuel Cornejo’s chronology (https://boleravel.fr/wp-content/uploads/RAVEL_Chronology_2018.pdf) dates the composition to 5 September 1908 and the première, by Viñes at the Société nationale, to 9 January 1909.

cues.title: The bell between two hands
cues.text: Ravel spreads the piano across three staves. High chords and low chords move around the B♭, which passes between the hands. Even where the chords fill the keyboard, the repeated note keeps sounding inside them.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 18: three-stave writing, alternating m.d. and m.g. indications for the bell, with chordal lines above and below.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A voice without expression
cues.text: A bare upper melody stands above the bell. Ravel marks it un peu en dehors, mais sans expression: slightly brought out, but without expression. The B♭ continues below, indifferent to the melody’s rise and fall.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 19, first system: pp un peu en dehors, mais sans expression over the repeated low B♭.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The chords return
cues.text: The piano fills out again in long, tied chords. The bell threads between them, still B♭. Ravel’s instruction from the first page remains in force: “without hurrying or slowing to the end”.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 19, lower systems. Ravel’s instruction Sans presser ni ralentir jusqu’à la fin appears on p. 17; our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A Bechstein in the Kaisersaal
cues.text: OE1FEU recorded this piece themselves, on a Bechstein D 282 concert grand in Vienna’s Kaisersaal, and dates it 3 April 2020. The recording is released under a Creative Commons Attribution–ShareAlike licence.
cues.evidence: Commons file description (own work, Bechstein Konzertflügel D 282, Wiener Kaisersaal, date 2020-04-03, licence CC BY-SA 4.0): https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Maurice_Ravel-_Gaspard_de_la_Nuit-_II_Le_Gibet.flac

cues.title: The bell remains
cues.text: The last page lets the melodic fragments fall silent. Deep held notes remain under the bell, and the final bars shrink to ppp. The repeated B♭ lasts until the last chord.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 20: low held bass, repeated B♭ and final ppp chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Chords surround the bell
transitions.to: B · Chords above and below the bell
transitions.how: The piano opens into three staves: low held notes, the recurring B♭ and chords high above it. The two hands share the bell while the upper chords are marked très lié, very smoothly joined. Its repeated pitch carries through each change of harmony.
transitions.evidence: Durand score (1909), pp. 18–19: three-stave writing and the continuing B♭.

transitions.title: A melody above the low bell
transitions.from: B · Chords above and below the bell
transitions.to: C · A bare melody, without expression
transitions.how: The fuller chords recede. A single upper line, marked pp and sans expression, crosses above the B♭ in the bass. Its long notes stretch across several tolls of the bell.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, p. 19, first two systems: exposed melody and low repeated B♭.

transitions.title: The chords close round B♭
transitions.from: C · A bare melody, without expression
transitions.how: The single upper line broadens into tied chords as the six-flat key signature returns. The B♭ bell continues between the hands, above a sustained low bass. Small crescendos swell the chords without changing the slow pace.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, p. 19, third and fourth systems: six-flat signature, tied chords and crescendo hairpins.

transitions.title: The melody leaves the bell
transitions.to: Coda · The bell outlasts the melody
transitions.how: The high chords diminish and the piano returns to the opening’s slow bell-and-chord writing. Deep sustained notes support B♭ octaves; the repeated figure grows softer through p, pp and ppp. Ravel keeps the same pace to the end.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, p. 20; the instruction to keep the pace appears on p. 17.

composer.epithet: He made a ballet from two tunes and a snare drum, and gave his war dead a suite of dances.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery. His mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He kept returning to the Basque coast, and Spain kept returning in his music: the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera that rocks through the Rapsodie espagnole, the clocks ticking in a Toledo shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. Two teachers then understood him: André Gedalge, who gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and Fauré, whose composition class he entered in January 1898. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, became the pianist his music needed. Viñes gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces their composer could never have played with comparable command.
